Vaginismus (involuntary, painful guarding of the vaginal musculature) is the most specific and likely diagnosis given the hallmark symptom of penetration-related tightness and its well-documented association with secondary infertility due to avoidance or inability to achieve intercourse. Pelvic Floor Hypertonicity Disorder is highly plausible as a broader pathophysiological framework encompassing vaginismus and contributing to both dyspareunia and reflexive sympathetic inhibition of erection. Psychogenic or mixed-etiology Erectile Dysfunction is very plausible given the bidirectional impact of sexual pain and performance anxiety in couples trying to conceive. Primary Ovarian Insufficiency is less likely: while it causes infertility, it does not explain the pelvic floor tension or dyspareunia; absence of reported menstrual irregularities, hot flashes, or elevated FSH makes it low probability. Endometriosis is possible but less likely without classic symptoms (e.g., cyclic pelvic pain, heavy periods, bowel/bladder symptoms); isolated dyspareunia can occur, but the dominant feature here is muscular tightness—not deep infiltrative or inflammatory pain—and no mention of other endometriosis-associated findings."}

Vaginismus (primary) best explains lifelong tightness preventing penetration and triggering anticipatory anxiety that secondarily affects the partner’s erection — supported by absence of consistent erectile failure. GPPPD is the DSM-5 umbrella diagnosis encompassing vaginismus and dyspareunia with behavioral avoidance; its high confidence reflects diagnostic alignment with ICD-11/DSM-5 criteria. Psychogenic, situational ED is highly likely given the intermittent nature and clear contextual link to partner’s discomfort and performance pressure. Mixed infertility is included because 15 months meets WHO infertility definition, and while no overt organic causes are described, subtle ovulatory or semen parameters may coexist — though current symptoms point more strongly to functional barriers. Confidence scores reflect clinical prevalence, symptom concordance, and absence of red flags for organic disease (e.g., no hormonal symptoms, no history of trauma/surgery, no chronic medical conditions)."}
